passage:
"I'm not taking the bus any more, Ma'am. I'll walk."
"It's six kilometres, Jeevan."
"Fine. Since the thing on the bus, I just... what if it happens again? In front of everyone?"
Rekha Ma'am nodded. "So now you're scared of the fear itself."
"Yeah. Even thinking about the bus, my heart starts."
"Did the doctor check you afterwards?"
"Yes. Said my heart's fine."
"Good. So here's what happened on the bus. Your body fired its alarm, like a smoke detector going off for burnt toast. Racing heart, dizzy, sure something awful was happening. Very scary. But it passed, didn't it?"
"In a few minutes."
"Right. Avoiding the bus teaches your brain the bus is dangerous. Understanding the alarm shrinks it. Want to try one stop with your friend on Monday?"
Jeevan picked at his sleeve. "One stop. Maybe."

qa.q: How far is the walk Jeevan wants to take instead of the bus?
qa.a: It's six kilometres.

qa.q: What is Jeevan most afraid of now?
qa.a: Jeevan dreads another panic episode happening on the bus in front of everyone.

qa.q: What small step did Rekha Ma'am suggest, and why?
qa.a: Riding just one stop with a friend on Monday, because avoiding the bus teaches the brain it is dangerous, while understanding the alarm shrinks it.

qa.q: How does Rekha Ma'am see what happened on the bus?
qa.a: Rekha Ma'am sees it as the body's alarm going off like a smoke detector for burnt toast: very scary, but it passes.

grounding: A teen avoids the bus for fear of another panic episode, and understanding what panic is begins to loosen that fear.

subtype: Teen scared of the fear itself [Actor]
passage: After I panicked in the school canteen in March, I stopped going anywhere crowded. First the canteen, then the assembly hall, then even the back of the maths room felt risky. I wasn't scared of the canteen. I was scared of my own heart speeding up. Every flutter felt like the start of another attack. My brother Siddharth noticed I was eating lunch in the corridor by the washrooms. "Vasudha, what's going on?" I told him. Our doctor had already checked me and said my body was healthy, so we sat and read the leaflet the school counsellor had given out about panic. It said the racing heart and the dizziness are the body's alarm, frightening but passing. I read it about ten times. Understanding it didn't fix everything, but the next week I sat in the canteen for five minutes, with Siddharth. My heart raced. It passed. I stayed.

qa.q: Where did Siddharth notice Vasudha eating lunch?
qa.a: In the corridor by the washrooms.

qa.q: What was Vasudha really scared of?
qa.a: Vasudha was afraid of the racing heart itself, treating every flutter as the start of another attack.

qa.q: What helped Vasudha go back to the canteen?
qa.a: Reading the counsellor's leaflet about what panic is, then returning for five minutes with Siddharth and letting the racing heart pass.

qa.q: What might Siddharth have felt when he found Vasudha in the corridor?
qa.a: Siddharth was probably worried and puzzled, which is why he asked what was going on and then sat with Vasudha.

grounding: A teen dreads another panic episode and avoids crowded places until understanding what panic is loosens its grip.

passage:
Tuesday: Two weeks after her heart raced on the crowded school bus, Sangeeta asked her father, Hemant, to drive her again. 'What if it happens on the bus?' she said. Hemant agreed, a little worried.
Thursday: The school counsellor drew a wave on paper. 'Panic rises, peaks and falls. It feels dangerous, but it isn't. Running away teaches your brain the bus is a threat.' Sangeeta frowned. 'So avoiding it keeps it going?' 'Often, yes.'
The next Monday: Sangeeta got on the bus with her friend Neha. At the second stop, her heart began to race. She held the rail, whispered 'wave,' breathed out slowly and let it rise. It peaked. Then, slowly, it fell. At school she texted Hemant: 'Rode the bus. It came and went.'

qa.q: What did the counsellor draw on paper?
qa.a: A wave.

qa.q: What was Sangeeta worried about on Tuesday?
qa.a: She was afraid that the racing heart would happen again on the bus.

qa.q: What helped Sangeeta get back on the bus?
qa.a: Understanding that panic rises and falls, and letting the wave pass instead of running from it.

qa.q: How might Hemant feel reading Sangeeta's text?
qa.a: He is likely to feel proud and relieved that she faced the bus and managed the feeling.

grounding: Shows a teenager who, after a panic episode, avoids the bus for fear of another, and how understanding panic loosens its grip.

passage: Tushar, you think I always went to the market alone? Listen to your Tanvir Chacha. When I was sixteen, in the crowded Friday bazaar, my heart suddenly pounded, my hands went numb, and I was sure I'd faint in front of everyone. It passed, but after that I was afraid of the fear. I stopped going to the bazaar. Then to the cinema. Then I would only take the bus if it was empty. My world got smaller and smaller. One day the school games teacher saw me walking the long way round and asked why. I told him. He said, 'That's panic. It can't harm you, but running from it makes it bigger.' So I went back, a little at a time, with my friend Rashid. First the edge of the bazaar. Then the middle. The fear came, and it went.

qa.q: Where was Tanvir when his heart first pounded?
qa.a: In the crowded Friday bazaar.

qa.q: What was young Tanvir feeling after that first episode?
qa.a: He was afraid of the fear itself, dreading another wave, so he avoided more and more places.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Tanvir's story?
qa.a: The games teacher explained it was panic and that running from it made it bigger, and Tanvir went back step by step with Rashid.

qa.q: How might the games teacher have seen young Tanvir walking the long way round?
qa.a: The teacher noticed something was wrong and was curious and concerned enough to ask.

grounding: Shows, through an elder's story, a teenager who after a panic episode avoids crowds and buses, and how understanding panic loosens its grip.

subtype: Teen scared of the fear itself [Actor]
passage: The board exam was tomorrow, and Aparna hadn't sat in the big hall since the assembly in March, when her heart had pounded and the room had spun. Since then she'd done tests in the staff room. Now there was no choice, and her mother was away at a cousin's wedding in Pune. At nine at night she sat on the stairs, shaking. 'What if it happens during the exam?' Her brother Madhav, home from college, sat beside her. 'What did the counsellor say it was?' 'Panic. Adrenaline. It rises and falls. It can't hurt me.' 'And what happens when you avoid it?' Aparna sighed. 'It gets stronger.' 'So tomorrow, if it comes, what will you do?' 'Breathe out slow. Let it peak. Keep writing.' Madhav nodded. In the morning he walked her to the gate. Her heart raced once, and she let it.

qa.q: Where was Aparna's mother?
qa.a: Away at a cousin's wedding in Pune.

qa.q: What was Aparna feeling on the stairs the night before?
qa.a: She was frightened of panicking during the exam and shaking at the thought.

qa.q: How did Madhav help without giving the answers himself?
qa.a: He asked questions so Aparna could remember in her own words what the counsellor had taught her, and made a plan.

qa.q: How might Madhav have felt walking her to the gate?
qa.a: He was probably a little nervous for her, but proud and hopeful.

grounding: Shows a teenager who, after a panic episode, avoids the exam hall for fear of another, and how understanding what panic is loosens its grip.

subtype: Teen scared of the fear itself [Actor]
passage: Since the panic episode on the crowded school bus in March, Vidya had found reasons not to take it. She walked forty minutes in the Chennai heat, claimed headaches on trip days, and even avoided the assembly hall because it felt too packed. Every time she imagined the bus, her chest tightened, and she worried the pounding heart would come back. The doctor had already checked that her heart was fine. Her cousin Akash, who'd had panic attacks in college, sat with her one evening. 'It's your body's alarm going off with no fire,' he said. 'Horrible, but it passes. The more you run from it, the louder it gets.' With the school counsellor's help, Vidya started with two stops, then three.

qa.q: How long did Vidya walk instead of taking the bus?
qa.a: Forty minutes, in the Chennai heat.

qa.q: What was Vidya afraid of?
qa.a: She was scared the pounding heart would come back, so she dreaded the feeling itself.

qa.q: What helped loosen the panic's grip?
qa.a: Understanding it as a false alarm that passes, and facing the bus in small steps with the counsellor's help.

qa.q: How might Akash have felt sharing his own experience?
qa.a: Akash probably felt protective and understanding, wanting to spare Vidya the fear he had lived through.

grounding: A teenager who fears another panic episode starts avoiding buses and crowds, and understanding panic loosens its grip.
